metricsHelp.score: Sums up the run in a number from 0 to 100, combining how many answers are right and how quick they are. Use it to compare runs of the same patient, not to compare them with other people.
metricsHelp.performance: The same result expressed from 0 to 1. The system uses it to choose the difficulty for next time: about 0.75 means the exercise was at the right difficulty.
metricsHelp.ability: The difficulty level (L1 to L5) the patient can handle in this activity. Unlike the score, it accounts for how hard the exercises were, so it is the best measure for following progress.
metricsHelp.accuracy: Share of correct responses over all trials. Higher is better.
metricsHelp.hits: Number of correct responses to stimuli that required a response.
metricsHelp.omissions: Stimuli that required a response but were not answered in time. Many omissions may reflect lapses of attention or slowness. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.commissions: Responses given when the patient should NOT respond (false alarms). They reflect impulsivity or poor inhibition. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.commissionRate: Share of "don't press" stimuli the patient responded to anyway. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.dPrime: How well the patient tells the stimuli to respond to from those to ignore, regardless of how often they press. 0 = responds at random; above 2 = tells them apart well. Higher is better.
metricsHelp.criterion: Response style. Positive = cautious (presses little: fewer false alarms but more omissions). Negative = impulsive (presses often: more false alarms). Close to 0 = balanced. It is not a grade: it describes the strategy.
metricsHelp.medianRt: The typical response time of correct answers, in milliseconds (1000 ms = 1 second): half the responses are faster, half slower. A few very slow responses do not distort it. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.meanRt: Mean reaction time (ms) of correct responses, excluding anticipations and outliers.
metricsHelp.rtCv: How irregular response times are (variability divided by the mean). Very irregular times are typical of attention that comes and goes. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.exgMu: The patient's usual speed when focused, not counting occasional slow responses. Computed only with at least 40 responses.
metricsHelp.exgSigma: How much the usual times vary among themselves: the lower, the steadier the responses.
metricsHelp.exgTau: How many responses are much slower than usual, and by how much. A high value points to frequent moments of distraction. Lower is better. Computed only with at least 40 responses.
metricsHelp.anticipations: Responses faster than 150 ms: too fast to be a reaction to the stimulus, so given "in advance". They are excluded from timing measures.
metricsHelp.postErrorSlowing: How much the patient slows down right after an error (ms). A positive value is a good sign: they notice the error and pay more attention.
metricsHelp.vigilanceRtSlope: How many milliseconds response times grow for each minute of exercise. Positive = the patient slows down as it goes on (fatigue or falling attention). Lower is better.
metricsHelp.fatigueIndex: Reaction times in the last third of the exercise divided by those in the first third. Above 1 = slows down towards the end.
metricsHelp.baselineRt: In the initial warm-up the patient presses as soon as a circle appears: it measures hand speed and device delay, with nothing to decide.
metricsHelp.decisionTime: The time to recognise the stimulus and decide, net of hand and device speed: reaction time in the exercise minus that of the initial warm-up. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.holdMedian: Median press duration (ms): how long the finger or key stays down. Very long or irregular presses may reflect motor aspects.
metricsHelp.pairs: Number of pairs on the board.
metricsHelp.attempts: Attempts: each attempt turns over two cards. Fewer attempts = better memory.
metricsHelp.efficiency: Pairs ÷ attempts. 1 would mean always matching at the first try, which is impossible even with perfect memory (cards must be discovered first).
metricsHelp.efficiencyVsOptimal: Attempts of optimal play with perfect memory ÷ the patient's attempts. 100% = like a player who forgets nothing; 50% = twice the attempts needed. Higher is better.
metricsHelp.memoryErrors: Memory errors: the patient had already seen the matching card but did not pick it. This is the error most directly tied to visual memory. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.perseverations: Perseverations: the same wrong pairing repeated more than once. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.secondsPerPair: Average seconds spent per pair found. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.medianFlipInterval: Median time between the first and second card of each attempt (ms).
metricsHelp.targets: Number of targets on the sheet.
metricsHelp.hitRate: Share of targets found. Higher is better.
metricsHelp.cancellationsPerMin: Targets found per minute: speed of visual exploration. Higher is better.
metricsHelp.cocX: Balance between left and right in the targets found, from −1 to +1. 0 = balanced; negative = found mostly on the left (missed on the right); positive = the opposite. It describes what happened; it is not a diagnosis.
metricsHelp.cocY: Balance between top and bottom in the targets found, from −1 to +1. 0 = balanced; negative = found mostly at the top.
metricsHelp.leftOmissions: Targets missed in the left half of the sheet.
metricsHelp.rightOmissions: Targets missed in the right half of the sheet.
metricsHelp.bestR: How orderly the search is, i.e. whether it follows rows or columns as in reading. Close to 1 = very orderly; close to 0 = jumps from one place to another. Higher is better.
metricsHelp.intersectionRate: Joining the targets in the order they were found, how many times the line crosses itself (per target found). Many crossings = disorderly search. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.meanDistance: Average distance between one cancellation and the next, relative to the sheet diagonal. Long jumps suggest a less systematic search. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.firstMarkX: Horizontal position of the first target cancelled (−1 = left edge, +1 = right edge): where exploration starts.
metricsHelp.medianInterval: Median time between one cancellation and the next (ms).
metricsHelp.selfCorrections: Times the patient undid one of their own responses: a sign of self-monitoring.
metricsHelp.durationS: Duration of the exercise in seconds.
metricsHelp.pcuScore: For each sequence, the share of items recalled in the right position, even when the whole sequence was not correct; then the average. It says more than plain right/wrong. Higher is better.
metricsHelp.maxSpan: Length of the longest sequence repeated without errors.
metricsHelp.spanEstimate: The sequence length the patient recalls with good confidence: the sequence gets longer after 3 right answers and shorter after a mistake, until it settles near their limit. Higher is better.
metricsHelp.itemErrors: Item errors: the patient pointed at something that was not in the sequence. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.orderErrors: Order errors: right items in the wrong position. They show difficulty keeping the serial order. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.firstPositionAccuracy: Accuracy on the first item of the sequences (primacy effect).
metricsHelp.lastPositionAccuracy: Accuracy on the last item of the sequences (recency effect).
metricsHelp.responseLatency: Time between the end of the sequence and the first tap (ms). Lower is better.
metricsHelp.interTapMedian: Median time between taps while the patient repeats the sequence (ms).
metricsHelp.errors: Wrong responses (excluding time-outs). Lower is better.
metricsHelp.timeouts: Stimuli the patient did not answer in time. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.perseverativeErrors: Perseverative errors: after a rule change the patient keeps applying the previous rule. They reflect cognitive rigidity. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.switchCostRt: Switch cost: how much slower (ms) the patient is on the trial right after a rule change compared with the others. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.switchCostAccuracy: How much accuracy drops on rule-change trials compared with the others. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.timeA: Time to connect the numbers-only sequence (part A), in seconds. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.timeB: Time for the alternating numbers–letters sequence (part B), in seconds. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.errorsA: Circles tapped by mistake in part A.
metricsHelp.errorsB: Circles tapped by mistake in part B.
metricsHelp.bMinusA: B − A difference: the extra time required by alternating, net of visuo-motor speed. It reflects cognitive flexibility. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.bOverA: B ÷ A ratio: like B − A, but relative to the patient's baseline speed. Lower is better.
metricsHelp.medianLinkA: Median time per link in part A (ms).
metricsHelp.medianLinkB: Median time per link in part B (ms).
metricsHelp.pauses: Links that took much longer than usual (over 2.5 times the median): hesitations or losing track.
metricsHelp.pathEfficiency: Movement efficiency (mouse/pen): straight-line distance ÷ actual pointer path. 1 = direct movement; low values = hesitations and corrections. Higher is better.
metricsHelp.backward: 1 if the sequence had to be repeated backwards.
metricsHelp.digits: 1 if the sequence used digits instead of squares.

help.abilityChart: The blue line is the level the patient handles successfully, updated after each run. The light band shows the uncertainty: wide at first, it narrows with practice and widens again after long breaks. Grey dots are the difficulties offered, chosen a little below the ability so the patient succeeds in about 3 trials out of 4.
help.metricChart: Each dot is a run; the line is the trend, a "soft" average that follows the general direction without chasing every dot.
help.trend: "Improving" or "Declining" appear only when the change is clear enough that it cannot be put down to chance; otherwise "Stable". At least 5 runs are needed.
help.slope30: How much the measure changes on average every 30 days; single runs very different from the others do not distort it. "Probably between … and …" is the margin of uncertainty: if it includes zero, you cannot say whether the measure is really changing.
help.changeFromBaseline: Difference between the average of the last 3 runs and that of the first 3. If the "probably between … and …" margin does not include zero, the difference is reliable.
help.domainChart: For each cognitive area, how many difficulty levels the patient has gained on average since the first time they did the activities of that area (weekly average). 0 = same as at the start; +1 = handles exercises one level harder.
help.profileChart: Mean ability per cognitive area on two chosen dates: grey is the start date, blue the end date. Useful to see at a glance where the patient grew most.
help.calendarChart: How many runs were done each day: shows how regular the work is.
help.excludeFlagged: Leaves unreliable runs out of the charts: interrupted (tab hidden for long), not completed, with many anticipations or too few trials. They stay visible in the run list.
help.inputDevice: Mouse, touch and pen have different delays (even tens of milliseconds): to compare times over time it is best to look at one device type.
help.trialsChart: Each dot is a trial. Circles = correct responses, triangles = errors, diamonds = anticipations or outliers (left out of timing measures).
help.distributionChart: How many correct responses fell in each time band. The curve separates usual speed (μ, where the peak is) from slow responses (τ, the "tail" on the right, linked to moments of distraction).
help.rawEvents: Every tap, time and movement recorded during the run. It allows replaying the path and recomputing measures if formulas improve. It is deleted automatically after the practice's retention period; summary measures are kept.
help.replay: Rebuilds the exercise exactly as it was and shows the patient's choices in order.
help.difficulty: Adaptive: the system picks the level from the estimated ability, so the patient succeeds in about 75% of trials (editable in the patient profile). Fixed: always uses the given level; with the lock open it is only the starting point for a new patient.
help.abilityLock: Locks this activity's difficulty for the patient: every session uses that level until you unlock it. Ability is still estimated.
help.levels: Difficulty ranges from L1 (very easy) to L5 (very hard), with intermediate values (e.g. L2.5). Each activity turns the level into concrete parameters: number of items, timing, similarity between stimuli.
help.quality: Automatic notes on run quality (interruptions, anticipations, too few trials…): they help judge whether a result is reliable.
